\section[patientia, patientiae]{patientia, patientiae — patience}

\label{lesson:LA-C174-patientia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for the liver, then the Latin for a kidney.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: patientia, patientiae}
\textbf{patientia, patientiae} — \textquotedblleft{}patience\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{patientia} is built on \emph{patior}, \textquotedblleft{}to suffer\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), through \emph{patiēns}, \textquotedblleft{}enduring\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{-ia}, an ending for a quality.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[lacrima, lacrimae]{lacrima, lacrimae — a tear}

\label{lesson:LA-C174-lacrima}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a kidney, then the Latin for patience.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lacrima, lacrimae}
\textbf{lacrima, lacrimae} — \textquotedblleft{}a tear\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lacrima} is inherited, usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*dakru-}, \textquotedblleft{}tear\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1). Old Latin had \emph{dacruma} with d (Lewis \& Short); Greek \emph{dakry}, \textquotedblleft{}tear\textquotedblright{}, and English \emph{tear} are cousins.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[animus, animī]{animus, animī — mind, spirit}

\label{lesson:LA-C174-animus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a laugh, then the Latin for a voice.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: animus, animī}
\textbf{animus, animī} — \textquotedblleft{}mind, spirit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{animus} is inherited, usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*h2enh1mos}, \textquotedblleft{}breath\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{*h2enh1-}, \textquotedblleft{}to breathe\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1); Greek \emph{anemos}, \textquotedblleft{}wind\textquotedblright{}, is a cousin (Lewis \& Short). \emph{anima}, \textquotedblleft{}breath, soul\textquotedblright{}, is its partner.
\end{cousinweb}
